confirmed.title: Per-part stress/strain/beam CSV and motion CSV use std::fixed<<setprecision(6): strains below 5e-7 become 0.000000 and close state times merge
confirmed.mechanism: writePartCSV: `ofs << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6) << point.time << "," << point.max_value << "," << point.min_value << "," << point.avg_value` (line 49-53). writeMotionCSV does the same at line 78 for Time/Avg_Disp_*/Avg_Vel_*/Avg_Acc_*/Max_Disp_Mag. With fixed(6), any value |v|<5e-7 prints as 0.000000, values around 1e-6 keep one significant digit, and times closer than 1e-6 print the same. The JSON keeps the same data at fixed(8), so the two outputs disagree.
confirmed.scenario: Real production output /data/koopark/Test_Impact_A/deep_reports/Run_20260603_071717_fab346: analysis_result.json strain_history gives part 1 global_max 1.9e-07 and global_min -2.8e-07, part 12 2.3e-07, part 22 3.2e-07. strain/part_N_eff_plastic_strain.csv is 0.000000 in 992/992 rows for 22 of 24 parts. In /data/koopark/Test_hs_shell_e2e (battery deck), strain/part_30_von_mises_strain.csv is only 0.000000 or 0.000001 across all 22 states, while the JSON global_max is 9.5e-07. part_100_max_principal_strain.csv shows peak 0.000011 against the JSON's 1.066e-05. Time: the last two states 0.00500000 and 0.00500002 both print as 0.005000. In Test_Impact_A stress/part_10_von_mises.csv and motion/part_1_motion.csv, 992 rows have only 987 distinct Time values (duplicates 0.000153, 0.000658, 0.000859, 0.000960, 0.001000). Test_Postprocess_v14 has 1980 rows and 1975 distinct times. For an SI (m) deck, a max displacement of 3e-7 m prints as 0.000000.
confirmed.consumers: koo_sphere_report/loader.py _load_stress_strain_csv (lines 244-265) takes true_peak/true_peak_time from these CSVs for von_mises, max/min principal stress, eff_plastic_strain, von_mises_strain and max/min principal strain. These feed the all-angle sphere report peak tables and curves. _load_motion_csv takes true_peak_g and true_peak_disp from the motion CSV. koo_impact_report/loader.py (line 1324) builds the impactor trajectory times and velocities from motion CSV. payload/analytics.py derives FFT/SRS dt from np.diff of those quantized times. koo_deep_report d3plot_reader._parse_motion_csv reads the motion curves.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Write CSV numbers as significant digits, not fixed decimals (for example `std::defaultfloat << std::setprecision(10)` or `std::scientific << setprecision(9)`), as writeSurfaceStrainCSV and set-report CSVs already do. Apply this to writePartCSV, writeMotionCSV, writeSurfaceCSV, writeQualityCSV and the tensor CSV. Add a test that round-trips 3e-9 and the time pair 1.5e-7/1.4e-7.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute the claim. The mechanism is real and production code reaches it, but I rate it medium, not high.

What holds up:
- At 36ea5db, writePartCSV (line 49), writeMotionCSV (line 78) and writeSurfaceCSV (line 117) all write with `std::fixed << std::setprecision(6)`. Any value below 5e-7 prints as 0.000000, and times closer together than 1e-6 print the same.
- The CSV files the claim cites match its numbers exactly.
- Production code reads these CSVs. koo_sphere_report's `_load_stress_strain_csv` takes `true_peak` and `true_peak_time` from the Max_ column. `_load_motion_csv` takes `true_peak_g` and `true_peak_disp`. koo_impact_report's `load_per_part_motions` gets `peak_g` and `t_peak_g` from motion CSV rows, and its trajectory loader (line 1324) reads Time and velocity. koo_deep_report's `_parse_outputs` gets its motion curves from `_parse_motion_csv`.

Why the damage is smaller than claimed:
1. The zeroed Test_Impact_A eff_plastic_strain values are noise, not real plastic strain. They run ±1e-7 to 1e-8 and include negative values, which plastic strain cannot have, so 0 is arguably the right reading.
2. The worst real case found is a 1.066e-05 principal strain printed as 0.000011, about 3% off. The 9.5e-07 strain printing as 0.000001 is similar.
3. The Test_Impact_A decks (all 15 decks sampled) save a state every ~1.01e-6 s, right at the rounding step. That gives 5 duplicate times in 992 rows. Peak times are off by at most about 0.5e-6 s.
4. The time-based calculations mostly survive:
   - The FFT drops zero gaps (`dts>0`) and averages the rest, so its sampling rate is off by only about 0.5% (987 of 991 gaps).
   - The shock response spectrum uses the median gap, which stays at 1e-6.
   - The sphere report's dσ/dt JavaScript skips zero gaps with `if (dt > 0)`.

It becomes serious only in less common cases: states saved less than 1e-6 s apart, which merge in bulk and can drive the median gap to 0; small elastic strains around 1e-6 to 1e-5; or SI decks where displacements under 1e-5 m keep one or two digits. So the numbers that reach users are slightly wrong for realistic inputs, and badly wrong only for uncommon inputs.

The mechanism is real, and the claim's example data checks out against production outputs on disk. It is not "high", though. With realistic inputs, the numbers users see change only a little.

1. **Code confirmed at 36ea5db.** writePartCSV (lines 49-55) and writeMotionCSV (line 78) both use `std::fixed << std::setprecision(6)`. writePartCSV writes every stress/ and strain/ CSV (called at lines 292-339 and 461). The JSON global_max is written at fixed(8) (AnalysisResult.hpp:512). A compiled test confirms the rounding:
   - 1.9e-7 and 4.9e-7 become 0.000000
   - 9.5e-7 becomes 0.000001
   - 1.066e-5 becomes 0.000011
   - 7.39e-6 becomes 0.000007
   - 0.00500000 and 0.00500002 both become 0.005000
   - 0.0863 (GPa) becomes 0.086300, which is fine
2. **Consumers confirmed.**
   - The sphere loader reads true_peak and true_peak_time from these CSVs (loader.py:423-452) and true_peak_g / true_peak_disp from the motion CSV.
   - The impact loader builds traj.times and velocities from the motion CSV (loader.py:1324).
   - The deep report reads stress and strain from the JSON, not the CSV. It reads only motion from the CSV.
3. **Why medium, not high.**
   - **(a) Normal decks lose little.** The sphere-type production run Test_Postprocess_v14 (1980 states, stresses 14-222 MPa, strains 7e-6 to 1.1e-2) was compared against its JSON for every stress and strain CSV. The worst peak error is 5.3%, on a strain of 7.39e-6 that became 7e-6. The next worst are 1.8% and 1.2%, and all stress errors are negligible.
   - **(b) The HTML already rounds more.** The sphere HTML shows strain with toFixed(4) or toFixed(5) (html_report.py:2938-2943). That hides most of the CSV loss, although rankings and colour maps still use the rounded raw values.
   - **(c) The all-zero plastic-strain parts are noise.** In Test_Impact_A, 22 of 24 eff_plastic_strain CSVs are all zero. But the JSON values for those parts are ±1e-7 with negative minimums, so they are numerical noise, not a real measurement that was lost.
   - **(d) Duplicate times are real but small.** Every production deck found writes a state about every 1.009e-6 s, which is exactly the 6-decimal resolution. That gives 5 duplicate times per 992 rows (Test_Impact_A) and 5 per 1980 rows (v14). The FFT uses the mean of the positive time steps, so its sample rate is off by only about 0.5%. The SRS uses the median, which is unaffected. The sphere loading-rate calculation skips zero time steps.
   - **(e) The severe case was not observed.** A seconds-unit deck that writes states more often than every 1e-6 s would collapse most times. That would be a real FFT and time-axis error, but I found no such deck.
   - **(f) Battery deck not affected.** The battery deck Test_hs_shell_e2e shows the strain loss, but its report is the deep report, which reads strain from the JSON.

So the loss is real and reachable in production. It does materially affect strains below about 1e-5, and times would collapse if a deck wrote states more often than every 1e-6 s. For typical decks the visible damage is small.

The mechanism is real and the files are used in production. Nothing later in the pipeline fixes it. writePartCSV and writeMotionCSV at 36ea5db write every number with std::fixed<<setprecision(6), so the smallest value they can show is 1e-6. The sphere report (koo_sphere_report/loader.py, around lines 229-274 and 418-452) takes stress, principal stress, plastic strain, von Mises strain, principal strain and motion curves and peaks only from these CSVs. It opens analysis_result.json only for metadata, and the JSON is cut to 20 points anyway. The impact report builds PartMotion.times and the impactor trajectory times from motion CSV. analytics._fft_dominant_freq uses the mean of the positive time steps and the SRS uses their median. The deep report reads stress and strain from JSON, which is not affected, but reads motion from CSV.

I checked the numbers on disk. In Test_hs_shell_e2e, JSON part 100 max_principal_strain 1.066e-05 is 1.1e-05 in the CSV, and part 30 vm_strain (JSON 9.5e-07) is only 0.000000 or 0.000001. In Test_Postprocess_v14, JSON eff_plastic_strain 7.39e-06 is 7e-06 in the CSV, and there are 1980 rows but only 1975 distinct times. All 28 motion-CSV output folders I found have repeated times, e.g. Test_Impact_A (JSON times 9.9e-07, 2e-06, 3.02e-06..., last pair 0.0009999/0.00100002 both 0.001000).

I lowered severity from high to medium. For the output on disk the errors are small or fall on parts that barely deform. Strains of 1e-3 to 1e-2 on the critical parts keep 3-5 significant digits, repeated times affect about 0.5% of rows, and the FFT sampling rate is off by less than 0.5%. Peak times move by at most 5e-7 s. Plastic strain below 5e-7 shows as 0, which physically is almost zero. The large failure only happens for output intervals of about 2e-7 s or less. That is inside the stated input range, but no such dataset exists on disk. In that case many states share one time string and the FFT dominant frequency comes out 10x too low (simulated below). The CSV and the JSON also disagree with each other.

confirmed.defect_class: 4/6. non-finite value written as invalid JSON (whole file unreadable)
confirmed.title: NaN/Inf are written as bare nan/inf in every JSON section except hotspot_clusters, which makes the whole analysis_result.json unparseable
confirmed.mechanism: timePointToJSON: `oss << std::fixed << std::setprecision(8); ... oss << "\"avg\": " << tp.avg_value` (485-490). The same raw operator<< is used in surfaceTimePointToJSON (565-591), doubleArrayToJSON (654-658), tensorToJSON (673-674), and in AnalysisTypes.hpp toExtendedJSON motion (724-726), element_quality (741-769, e.g. `", \"max_volume_change\": " << q.max_volume_change`), beam (791-796), set_reports (832) and surface_strain (865-876). iostream prints NaN as `nan`/`-nan` and infinity as `inf`, and none of these are valid JSON (Python accepts only NaN/Infinity). Only jnum() (689-699) maps non-finite values to null, and it is used only by the hotspot serializers. SinglePassAnalyzer sums element values with no isfinite filter (`stats.stress_sum += vm;`). Element-quality volume/area ratios are computed from current node coordinates with no finiteness check, and `if (!tp.volume_measured || vol_ratio > tp.volume_change_max)` accepts inf.
confirmed.scenario: Reproduced by compiling the 36ea5db headers. First case: a stress point with avg_value = NaN emits `"avg": nan`, and Python json.loads fails with 'Expecting value: line 22 column 75'. Second case: an element_quality time point with volume_change_max = inf emits `"max_volume_change": inf` and the load fails. Realistic triggers: (a) a deck with erosion where freed nodes carry inf/nan coordinates, run with --element-quality. The repo itself documents that this happens in production decks: MotionAnalyzer.cpp:175-178/213-217, sphere loader.py:278-283, deep d3plot_reader.py:606-609. The hex/shell area ratio for an element touching such a node becomes inf/NaN. (b) An LS-DYNA run that error-terminates on NaN writes a final d3plot state with NaN solid stresses, so that state's avg becomes NaN. Either way one bad number makes the whole 20 MB result unreadable.
confirmed.consumers: koo_deep_report/core/d3plot_reader.py _parse_outputs (449-450, `raw = json.load(f)` with no try) aborts the whole deep report. koo_sphere_report/loader.py 397-398 and koo_impact_report/loader.py 98-99 use json.load and fail the run. campaign_metrics.py 182 also uses json.loads.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Route every double written into analysis_result.json through jnum() (non-finite becomes null, significant-digit formatting), including timePointToJSON, surfaceTimePointToJSON, doubleArrayToJSON, tensorToJSON and all toExtendedJSON blocks. Optionally also skip non-finite element values in SinglePassAnalyzer and in the element-quality ratios, and count them.

verdicts.reason:
The defect is real. At 36ea5db, `jnum()` is the only JSON writer that turns non-finite values into null, and only the hotspot serializers use it. Every other section streams doubles straight through `std::fixed`, so a NaN comes out as a bare `nan`. I compiled the 36ea5db headers and fed in `ExtendedAnalysisResult` with `avg_value = NaN`. The output contained `"avg": nan`, and Python's `json.load` failed with `Expecting value: line 22 column 77`. Nothing catches that error: deep `_parse_outputs` (line 450) has no try, and neither does sphere `load_simulation_result` (line 398), which `load_all` calls in an unguarded loop (lines 736-743). One bad run therefore aborts that run's deep report and the whole sphere campaign report.

Real solver output does contain NaN. `/data/koopark/Test_DTMIN_erode/dtmin_0p01` is an in-house erosion run whose d3hsp reports NaN energies, and its `d3plot19` holds 144 NaN float words (`0x7fc00000` and `0xffc00000`). Reading it with the kood3plot library gives 491 states. The last two states have 24 non-finite coordinate words and 24 non-finite velocity words (8 nodes), while the solid stresses are all finite (0 of 47257 elements).

The claim is only partly right about how the NaN reaches the JSON:
(1) The stress/strain history path needs NaN stresses. That did not happen in this deck, so it is plausible but not observed.
(2) Element quality: NaN coordinates alone usually do not reach the JSON for solids. `computeAspectRatio8` starts from `mn=1e30` and `mx=0`, so NaN edges are skipped. The scaled Jacobian skips NaN corners. A NaN `vol_ratio` is only adopted when `!tp.volume_measured`, i.e. when the NaN element is the first in its part. In this deck the 18 affected hexes sit at positions 1130 and later in part 21, so even `--element-quality` would write valid JSON here. The claim's point that `vol_ratio > max` "accepts inf" needs inf coordinates, and none were observed.
(3) There is a real propagation path for shells. `computeAspectRatio4` seeds `mn` and `mx` from `edges[0]`. If node 0 or node 1 has NaN coordinates, `mn` and `mx` stay NaN, both guards are false, and the function returns `{NaN, true}`. `ar_sum` then becomes NaN, `"ar_avg"` is written as `nan`, and the JSON cannot be parsed. I reproduced this in a standalone copy of the function. Element quality is a documented opt-in in `scripts/post_analyze.sh` (`--element-quality`).

The maintainer's later commit 63577f5 states this defect ("NaN 을 JSON 이 아닌 nan 으로 썼다") and moves `AnalysisResult.hpp` onto `jnum()`. The `toExtendedJSON` blocks in `AnalysisTypes.hpp` (motion, element_quality, beam, set_reports, surface_strain) still write raw doubles at HEAD. Severity is medium: the path runs in production, but it needs a run that went NaN, plus either NaN stresses or a shell deck run with the opt-in element-quality flag.

The defect is real. Every writer except jnum() streams doubles with a bare `<<`, so NaN comes out as `nan`/`-nan` and infinity as `inf`, and one such token makes Python's json.load reject the whole analysis_result.json. A real LS-DYNA erosion run on this machine writes float32 NaN into d3plot, and the reader passes it through unchanged. Two parts of the claim are wrong, though.
(1) Trigger (b), NaN solid stress, is unsupported. In the one real NaN deck found, only the coordinates and velocities of deleted nodes are NaN; the stress words are finite.
(2) Trigger (a) works differently for hexes than claimed. `vol_ratio > tp.volume_change_max` is false for NaN, and LS-DYNA writes NaN, not inf. So a hex volume ratio poisons the output only when the element with the deleted node is the first measured hex8 of its part.
The default pipeline at 36ea5db is protected on that deck: MotionAnalyzer skips non-finite values, set reports and the solid aspect ratio only ever compare values (a NaN comparison is false, so NaN never gets stored), surface faces use initial coordinates, and hotspots go through jnum(). I checked the real deck: all 18 hex8 elements touching NaN nodes are in material 21 and none is first in its part, so its JSON would still parse.
A concrete path that does reach JSON is --element-quality (an opt-in flag in the koo_deep_report CLI, also switched on by a `type: element_quality` job in the config) on a shell deck with node deletion. computeAspectRatio4 starts mn and mx from edges[0]. If node 0 or node 1 is NaN, both stay NaN and neither guard fires, so it returns {NaN, true}. Then `ar_sum += ar` turns `"ar_avg"` into `nan`, and the deep report's `raw = json.load(f)` aborts. So this is medium severity: a production path with an opt-in flag and an erosion deck. The failure is loud (the report does not load) rather than a silently wrong number.

confirmed.mechanism: `oss << ind2 << "\"global_max\": " << std::fixed << std::setprecision(8) << stats.globalMax()` (512-514). timePointToJSON sets `std::fixed << std::setprecision(8)` (485). The same applies in surfaceTimePointToJSON (565), doubleArrayToJSON (654, peak_element_tensors time/sxx..szx), and AnalysisTypes.hpp:865 surface_strain_analysis (`std::setprecision(8)` on a stream already set to std::fixed at 854). The file's own jnum() comment (692-697) describes exactly this loss ('ε_p(1e-6) 는 유효숫자 3자리만 … 1e-9 는 "0.00000000"'), but the fix was applied only to hotspots.

Test_Impact_A strain_history shows global_max 1e-08/2e-08 (1 significant digit) and part 19 `global_max 0.0` with `global_min -1e-08`, where the positive peak most likely rounded away.

confirmed.suggested_fix: Serialize with jnum() (setprecision(10), defaultfloat) instead of std::fixed<<setprecision(8) for all value and time fields in partStatsToJSON, timePointToJSON, surfaceTimePointToJSON, doubleArrayToJSON, tensorToJSON and the surface_strain block.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this claim. At 36ea5db the part history, surface history, tensor and surface strain JSON writers all format numbers with `std::fixed << std::setprecision(8)`. That keeps 8 digits after the decimal point, not 8 significant digits, so any value below 5e-9 prints as exact zero. Values around 1e-8 to 1e-6 keep only 1 to 3 significant digits. The code runs on the normal path: koo_deep_report launches unified_analyzer, then d3plot_reader.py `_parse_series` reads `global_max` and the per-point values. Those feed deep report `peak_strain` / `peak_vm_strain` (__main__.py 1333/1338) and impact loader.py 1244 and 1251-1265 (`peak_strain`, `peak_principal_strain`, `min_principal_strain`, `peak_vm_strain`).

Real production outputs show the loss:
- The Test_Impact_A deep_reports runs report strain_history peaks such as 1e-08 and 2e-08 (one significant digit). Parts 19, 24 and 25 show `global_max 0.0`.
- The battery run Test_hs_shell_e2e (SIF on node001) reports vm_strain 9.5e-07 and max_principal_strain 1.02e-06.

The only other place these numbers exist is the strain CSV, and it is coarser still. `part_19_eff_plastic_strain.csv` prints "0.000000" and "-0.000000" with an element ID attached, so the CSV cannot recover the value either.

The file's own `jnum()` comment (lines 692-697) describes exactly this loss, but the fix was applied only to the hotspot fields.

Why medium and not high: the absolute error is at most 5e-9 strain. Strains of about 1e-5 or more, which covers anything that matters for engineering, keep 4 or more significant digits. Stresses in GPa, MPa or Pa and times at 1e-7 s steps are not affected. So the damage is limited to near-zero-strain parts: their peaks come out as rounded or exact zero, and cross-run comparisons of those parts show visible steps. It is a real, reachable precision loss, but the numbers it changes carry little engineering meaning.

I could not refute this. The mechanism is real and runs in production. unified_analyzer writes analysis_result.json through `result.saveExtendedToFile` (examples/unified_analyzer.cpp:528). That calls the base `toJSON(true)` (AnalysisTypes.hpp:712), and every *_history block goes through `partStatsArrayToJSON`. That function and the per-point `timePointToJSON` use `std::fixed << std::setprecision(8)`, so each value is rounded to an absolute 1e-8. Strains below 5e-9 become 0.00000000, and values around 1e-8 to 1e-7 keep only 1 or 2 significant digits. The surface_strain_analysis block does the same thing (AnalysisTypes.hpp:854 sets std::fixed on the persistent `extra` stream, and :865 sets setprecision(8)).

Real production outputs have strains in exactly this range. In Test_Impact_A (992 states), strain_history global_max values are 1e-08, 2e-08, 4e-08 and so on (one significant digit). In Test_hs_shell_e2e, vm_strain global_max is 0.00000095, and data points show "max": 0.00000002. The file's own comment on jnum() (lines 692-697) names this exact loss, but the fix was only applied to hotspots.

Consumers read these numbers straight from the JSON: koo_deep_report `_parse_series` global_max -> __main__.py:1333/1338 peak_strain / peak_vm_strain and strain_ratio, and koo_impact_report loader.py `_extract_part_stress_strain` peak_strain, peak_principal_strain and peak_vm_strain. Revision-to-revision ratios or deltas get the relative error in full (1e-08 vs 2e-08 looks like 100%).

Two limits on the claim. First, the absolute error is at most 5e-9, which is usually negligible in engineering terms. Second, the peak_element_tensors part is weak: those arrays hold stress, and 1e-8 in GPa is 0.01 Pa, so they lose nothing meaningful for realistic units. Those limits keep this at medium, not high.

confirmed.defect_class: 4. silent placeholder reported as measured value
confirmed.title: element_quality per-point data[] drops the aspect/volume/skew/warp measured flags, so the deep report plots AR=0 and volume ratio=1.0 for unmeasured parts
confirmed.mechanism: `extra << "{\"time\": " ... << ", \"ar_max\": " << tp.aspect_ratio_max << ", \"ar_avg\": " << tp.aspect_ratio_avg << ", \"jac_measured\": " ... << ", \"skew_max\": " << tp.skewness_max << ", \"warp_max\": " << tp.warpage_max << ", \"vol_min\": " << tp.volume_change_min << ", \"vol_max\": " << tp.volume_change_max` (758-770). Only jac_measured is written per point. ElementQualityTimePoint has aspect_measured/volume_measured/skewness_measured/warpage_measured, but they are not serialized, so the defaults (aspect 0.0, volume 1.0, skew/warp 0.0) go out as values. writeQualityCSV correctly leaves these cells blank.
confirmed.scenario: Reproduced: a solid part whose elements are all tets stored as degenerate hex8 (common in drop models) has computeAspectRatio8 fail on its zero-length edge and distinct8=false. The per-point JSON is then {ar_max: 0.0, ar_avg: 0.0, vol_min: 1.0, vol_max: 1.0, skew_max: 0.0, warp_max: 0.0}, while the part-level aspect_measured=false and volume_measured=false. A tria-only shell part likewise gets skew_max/warp_max 0.0 at every state.
confirmed.consumers: koo_deep_report/report/html_report.py initQualityCharts (2011-2040) plots q.data.map(d=>d.ar_max / ar_avg / vol_min / vol_max / warp_max / skew_max) with no flag check. The user sees a flat AR=0 curve and a flat 'Volume/Area Change = 1.0' (no deformation) curve for tet parts, even though the summary table above correctly shows '—'. confirmed.suggested_fix: Serialize ar_measured/vol_measured/skew_measured/warp_measured per point (or write null via jnum when unmeasured) and have the charts skip unmeasured points.

verdicts.reason: The claimed defect is real. I checked it against commit 36ea5db. In toExtendedJSON, the per-state data[] entries include jac_measured but no measured flag for aspect ratio, skewness, warpage or volume, so the struct defaults are written as if they were real values. The defaults are aspect 0.0, skew/warp 0.0 and volume 1.0. In UnifiedAnalyzer.cpp, LS-DYNA tets and wedges are stored as hex8 with repeated nodes. For those elements computeAspectRatio8 returns {0.0,false} because one edge has zero length, and distinct8 is false. A part made only of such elements therefore never sets tp.aspect_measured or tp.volume_measured. Tria-only shells never set skewness_measured or warpage_measured. koo_deep_report's d3plot_reader.py passes eq["data"] through unchanged, and html_report.py initQualityCharts plots d.ar_max, ar_avg, vol_min and vol_max for every part (plus warp_max and skew_max for shells) without checking any flag. The result is a flat AR=0 curve and a flat volume ratio of 1.0 drawn on the y=1 dotted reference line, which reads as 'no change'. The summary table does check the part-level flags and shows '—', so it is partly protected, but the charts are not. writeQualityCSV leaves these cells blank, so the CSV is correct and only the JSON path has the problem. This is reachable in production when deep report runs with --element-quality (an opt-in flag) on models with tet-only or wedge-only solid parts or tria-only shell parts. I rate it medium, not high, because the flag is opt-in and the table next to the charts shows '—'.

I could not refute this claim. At 36ea5db, `toExtendedJSON` (include/kood3plot/analysis/AnalysisTypes.hpp:755-770) writes a `jac_measured` flag for each point, but no aspect, volume, skewness or warpage flag. When a metric was not measured, its default value is written as if it were real: ar_max/ar_avg 0.0, vol_min/vol_max 1.0, skew_max/warp_max 0.0.

The inputs that trigger this are realistic. LS-DYNA stores a tet as a hex8 with node 4 repeated (1,2,3,4,4,4,4,4). If a whole campaign was analyzed by one post-09-13 build (e.g. c6ef4ca, before the 36ea5db surface fix), the header shows a single build and no warning. The impact report has no such warning, and the deep report only prints a build line.

The user avoids stale results only by passing --force by choice. Default FORCE is false and SCHEMA_CHECK is true, so a default rerun still reuses them.

I rate this medium, not high. A wrong value reaches the user only when post_analyze is rerun on an existing campaign directory after an analyzer upgrade, without --force: for example adding runs, regenerating after a SIF update, or re-simulating a run in place. That workflow is realistic but conditional, and mixed campaigns get a small header warning. I did not find existing campaigns on /data/koopark (5-level search) whose .ua_schema markers predate the fixes. Under en_US.UTF-8, which is this host's LANG, it is Output2, so deep_reports/Run_x holds Output2's data. koo_impact_report's `_find_deep_output_dir` (loader.py lines 1930-1953) looks exactly at deep_reports/<run.name> and treats it as the run's Output data. A later impact run could therefore reuse the wrong group's analysis_result.json and motion CSVs. The default path is safe, because `run_step_unified` runs first and sets `_num_groups`=2. The same fallback is worse for the KooChainRun DWI layout (output/results/dwi_*/Run_*/Output/d3plot): in `--deep-only` mode every run name becomes "results", so all runs write to deep_reports/results and only the first is processed. Limits on severity: post_analyze.sh is the production orchestrator and `--deep-only` is a documented option. But of 403 real Runs under /data/koopark, none has a d3plot outside Output (the DynamicRelaxation folders hold only DropSet.k and dynaintoinitial.txt). Multi-group Runs are supported by the code (the Step 1 and sphere grouping logic) but I saw none in real data. Medium severity fits.

The claim holds for `--deep-only`. `_num_groups` is only set inside `run_step_unified` (line 443), and it is a global because it is not declared `local`. With `--deep-only`, lines 796-797 go straight to `run_step_deep`, so `${_num_groups:-1}` at line 685 falls back to 1. That makes both Run_x/Output/d3plot and Run_x/Output2/d3plot map to `deep_reports/Run_x`. koo_deep_report writes `<output>/result.json` (__main__.py:978), so the skip check at line 694 fires for the second group. The summary then counts that group under 스킵 (skipped), not 실패 (failed), so it looks like its report already exists. I reproduced this by pulling `run_step_deep` out of 36ea5db and running it against a stub koo_deep_report on a fake Run_a/Run_b × Output/Output2 tree. It ran 2 jobs and skipped 2, and `deep_reports/Run_{a,b}/result.json` came only from Output2, the group `sort` happened to put first in en_US.UTF-8. The Output group's deep reports were never made, and nothing shows which group the Run_x folder holds. Setting `_num_groups=2` gives 4 correct folders (`deep_reports/Output/Run_a`, etc.). The script clearly expects multi-group layouts: see the ANALYSIS_GROUPS comment 'Output, Output2 등' and the per-group sphere reports at line 577. post_analyze also ships in the SIF (build_module.sh:314), so production can reach this. Three caveats lower the impact. (1) In the default full run, `run_step_unified` runs before `run_step_deep` and sets `_num_groups`, so the bug needs `--deep-only`. It can also happen in IMPACT mode with no config, but IMPACT flat layouts only use one 'Output' group, where 1 is the right answer. (2) The impact consumer part of the claim is weak. `_find_deep_output_dir` looks at `run_dir/Output/report` first, and IMPACT DOE layouts have one group, so impact reports are hardly affected. (3) I found no multi-group test dir on disk (Test_010_Sequential_Quick only has Output). So it needs an uncommon but supported input. Medium severity.

confirmed.title: NARBS user-ID arrays read in the wrong order: shell, thick-shell and beam element IDs are shifted
confirmed.mechanism: The parser reads the ID blocks as nodes, solids, `// 3. Thick shell element IDs (NSORTT = NELT)` (l.79), `// 4. Beam element IDs` (l.91), `// 5. Shell element IDs` (l.103). The spec it cites (ls-dyna_database.txt l.728-732) gives the order NUSERN, NUSERH, NUSERB (beams), NUSERS (shells), NUSERT (thick shells). The NARBS header pointers agree with the spec: NSRB=NSRH+NEL8, NSRS=NSRB+NEL2, NSRT=NSRS+NEL4. GeometryParser::parse_narbs then copies these IDs into mesh.real_shell_ids / real_thick_shell_ids / real_beam_ids and into shells[i].id / thick_shells[i].id / beams[i].id.
confirmed.scenario: Real deck /data/battery_study/case_01_phase1_stacked_tier-1/d3plot has NARBS=23091, NEL4=7370, NELT=4704, and header pointers [-1, 9739, 10900, 10900, 18270, ...] (NSRT=18270=NSRS+NEL4). Reading it the parser's way assigns thick shells the IDs [393..8232], which are really shell IDs. Shells get [8233..10624], which is a mix of real shell and thick-shell IDs. Lasso and the spec give shells [393..12074] and thick shells [1..10624]. None of the 7370 shell IDs match. The same shift hits any deck with NARBS>0 and NELT>0 that also has shells or beams.
confirmed.consumers: Hotspot clusters for element_type shell/thick_shell take peak_element_id from mesh.real_shell_ids / real_thick_shell_ids (HotspotClusterAnalyzer.cpp:608-610, 870-872). confirmed.suggested_fix: Read the ID blocks in spec order: nodes, solids, beams, shells, thick shells. Better still, seek to each block with the header pointers (NSRH/NSRB/NSRS/NSRT). Add a regression test on a deck that has both shells and thick shells, and check the IDs against lasso.

confirmed.defect_class: 6 silent mis-selection (interior elements reported as surface)
confirmed.title: Exterior-face detection breaks on tets stored as degenerate hex8: interior tets land in the ±Z surface results and real boundary faces are missed
confirmed.mechanism: Each solid contributes 6 hex faces from HEXA_FACE_NODES, keyed by `generateFaceHash(face_nodes)` over the sorted 4 node indices, and `if (pair.second == 1)` marks a face exterior. LS-DYNA stores a tet as (A,B,C,D,D,D,D,D). Face 0 {0,3,2,1} then becomes the 4-node set {A,B,C,D}, which is unique to that element, so it always counts once and is always 'exterior'. The real faces ABC and ACD never appear as their own hash, so faces shared between tets never cancel. These faces have non-zero normals, so the zero-normal filter added in 36ea5db does not remove them.
confirmed.scenario: I replicated the algorithm exactly in Python on a 2x2x2 cube split into 48 Kuhn tets in (a,b,c,d,d,d,d,d) form. The true boundary has 48 triangles. The algorithm returns 144 'exterior' faces with non-zero normals, and 120 of them are interior. The +Z 45° filter picks 16 faces, 8 of them interior (elements 4,5,16,17,28,29,40,41). Surface von Mises max/avg for 'Top (+Z)' and 'Bottom (-Z)' therefore include interior elements, and boundary tets whose only outer face is ABC or ACD are dropped. The code's own comment notes MinimumModel.k is 76% tets.
confirmed.consumers: surface_defaults injects the ±Z SURFACE_STRESS/SURFACE_STRAIN jobs into every unified_analyzer run (UnifiedAnalyzer.cpp:135-155). Results go to surface/*_stress.csv, surface/*_strain.csv, analysis_result.json surface_analysis and surface_strain_analysis. Users read these raw outputs; the ±Z investigation behind 36ea5db started from them.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Build faces from each element's unique-node topology (tet: 4 triangles, wedge: 2 triangles + 3 quads, pyramid, hex). Hash triangles by their 3 sorted unique nodes. Drop faces with fewer than 3 unique nodes before counting.

verdicts.reason:
The claim holds. At 36ea5db, SurfaceExtractor::extractExteriorSurfaces treats every solid as a hex. It builds 6 four-node faces from HEXA_FACE_NODES (lines 99-106) and hashes each one by its 4 sorted node indices, keeping duplicates (generateFaceHash, lines 370-381). A face counts as exterior when its hash appears exactly once (line 130). The repo's own comments (UnifiedAnalyzer.cpp:838-842, HotspotClusterAnalyzer.cpp:132-137) confirm LS-DYNA stores a tet as (A,B,C,D,D,D,D,D).

For that pattern:
- Face 0 {0,3,2,1} hashes to the full node set {A,B,C,D}. Only that element can produce this hash, so it is always 'exterior'.
- That face's diagonal-cross normal, (C-A)x(B-D), is non-zero, so the zero-normal filter added in 36ea5db (filterByDirection, line 279) keeps it.
- The real triangles ABC and ACD are never hashed on their own, so they never cancel.
- ABD and BCD are hashed with a duplicate node, so they cancel only when the neighbour happens to repeat the same node.

UnifiedAnalyzer.cpp:135-155 adds the ±Z SURFACE_STRESS and SURFACE_STRAIN jobs by default (surface_defaults=true in AnalysisTypes.hpp:1081). Only koo_custom_report turns this off. Both job types call extractSolidExteriorSurfaces (UnifiedAnalyzer.cpp:558, SurfaceStrainAnalyzer.cpp:86), which uses this path. The results go to analysis_result.json (surface_analysis, surface_strain_analysis) and to the surface CSVs (unified_analyzer.cpp:466-481).

I re-implemented the algorithm and ran it on three meshes:
1. A synthetic Kuhn-tet cube, which reproduces the claim.
2. A random Delaunay tet mesh.
3. The real production deck /data/Tests/MinimumModel.k. Its 43,657 solids are 33,241 tets, 10,400 hexes and 16 wedges. Here the '+Z' surface picks 20,784 elements. 10,349 of them have no +Z boundary face, and 5,897 have no boundary face at all. It also misses 3,116 true top elements. '-Z' has 7,246 wrong and 364 missed.

The surface von Mises/strain max and avg, and the max element IDs, are therefore computed over a largely wrong element set. One mitigation: no Python HTML report renders surface_analysis. The wrong values sit in the raw JSON/CSV outputs of every deep, impact and sphere unified_analyzer run on tet decks. The ±Z surface investigation behind 36ea5db started from those outputs.

I could not refute this claim. I checked it three ways: I rebuilt the algorithm in Python, I ran the real `SurfaceExtractor` from `libkood3plot.a` on a real LS-DYNA tet d3plot, and I checked the connectivity in that file with lasso. None of the relevant files have changed since 36ea5db.

**How it goes wrong.** The code takes 6 hex faces per element (lines 99-109), hashes the sorted 4 node indices, and treats any hash seen once as exterior (lines 129-131). A tet is stored as (A,B,C,D,D,D,D,D). For a tet, face 0 {0,3,2,1} becomes the quad A,D,C,B, and its hash is the full set {A,B,C,D}. No other element has that set, so this face is always marked exterior, and its normal cross(C-A, B-D) is not zero. That means the `isZero` filter added in 36ea5db (lines 277-281) keeps it. The real triangles ABC and ACD never get their own hash. ABD and BCD are hashed with a repeated node (e.g. {A,B,D,D}), so a triangle shared by two tets only cancels if both tets repeat the same node. Nothing normalizes tets before this: GeometryParser::parse_solids copies the 8 node IDs as they are.

**Where it reaches users.** `surface_defaults` defaults to true (AnalysisTypes.hpp:1081), so every unified_analyzer run gets the ±Z SURFACE_STRESS and SURFACE_STRAIN jobs (UnifiedAnalyzer.cpp:135-155). Only koo_custom_report turns this off. The ±Z jobs call `extractSolidExteriorSurfaces` then `filterByDirection` (UnifiedAnalyzer.cpp:558, 568; SurfaceStrainAnalyzer.cpp:86-89; SinglePassAnalyzer.cpp:483-490). Results are written to analysis_result.json (`surface_analysis`, `surface_strain_analysis`) and to the surface CSVs (unified_analyzer.cpp:466-481).

**Why nothing else catches it.**
- Tet meshes are the normal case in production: HotspotClusterAnalyzer.cpp:135 notes that 76.1% of MinimumModel.k elements use this tet pattern.
- The project's own check, tests/surface/verify_surface_stress_lasso.py, uses the same "6 quad faces, count once" rule, so it would pass the wrong result.

**Caveat on severity.** No Python HTML report reads `surface_analysis` or the surface CSVs. Only the GUI job builder mentions them. The wrong numbers therefore reach users through the raw JSON/CSV outputs that every production run writes. Those are the outputs the ±Z investigation behind 36ea5db started from.

The claim holds. I reproduced it with the actual unified_analyzer binary on a real LS-DYNA tet deck, not only in a Python replica. The files involved (SurfaceExtractor.cpp, GeometryParser.cpp and the surface analyzers) have no commits or working-tree changes since 36ea5db, so the built binary runs the audited code.

How it breaks:
- GeometryParser::parse_solids keeps the raw 8-node connectivity. In the d3plot, a tet is stored as (A,B,C,D,D,D,D,D); lasso shows all 4000 tets of part 2 in ex02 stored this way.
- SurfaceExtractor hashes the 6 hex faces by their sorted node indices. Face 0 {0,3,2,1} becomes {A,B,C,D}, which no other element can share, so it always counts once and is treated as exterior. Its normal (C-A)x(B-D) is not zero, so the zero-normal filter added in 36ea5db does not remove it.
- The real triangles ABC and ACD are never hashed. As a result, shared ABD/BCD triangles often fail to cancel and some real boundary faces are missed.

Nothing later corrects this. SurfaceStressAnalyzer::analyzeState and SurfaceStrainAnalyzer use the filtered faces as they are, with no geometric check.

Reach: surface_defaults=true is the default. koo_deep_report's YAML builder writes no surface jobs and never sets surface_defaults=false; only koo_custom_report does. So every production run on a deck with tets writes wrong ±Z data to surface/*_stress.csv and *_strain.csv and to analysis_result.json (surface_analysis / surface_strain_analysis).

One point in the defect's favour on severity is also a limit. No Python HTML report at 36ea5db reads surface_analysis or the surface CSVs, so the wrong values reach users only through these raw JSON/CSV files and GUI-created surface_stress jobs, not through HTML reports. Tet meshes are common (the code notes MinimumModel.k is 76% tets), and the results are clearly wrong, not borderline.

confirmed.title: Element quality looks at only 10 evenly spaced states, so transient inversions and peak distortion are missed
confirmed.mechanism: `size_t n_samples = std::min(n_states, size_t(10));` ... `size_t idx = i * (n_states - 1) / (n_samples - 1);`. Only those states are analyzed. ElementQualityStats::computeGlobalStats then reports min_jacobian, max_negative_jacobian_count, min/max_volume_change and peak_aspect_ratio as extremes 'across all time'.
confirmed.scenario: A 992-state drop test is sampled at states 0,110,220,...,991. An element that inverts (scaled Jacobian < 0) only during states 130-170 of the impact is never evaluated. The output is max_negative_jacobian_count=0 and a min_jacobian from a calm state, and the report prints '음수Jac=0개'.
confirmed.consumers: analysis_result.json element_quality → koo_deep_report d3plot_reader.py:491 → the console summary AR/Jac/음수Jac (__main__.py:1399-1411) and the report. Also quality/part_*_quality.csv. Enabled by koo_deep_report --element-quality.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Evaluate every state, or at least track per-element extremes over all states (the states are already in memory). If sampling stays, record the sampled state count in the JSON and do not call the result a peak.

verdicts.reason: The claim holds. At 36ea5db, processElementQualityJobs has all_states in memory but only looks at up to 10 evenly spaced states (line 1649, not 1646). The per-sample points in `data` go to ElementQualityStats::computeGlobalStats (AnalysisTypes.hpp:307), which takes min_jacobian, max_negative_jacobian_count, peak_aspect_ratio, min/max_volume_change, peak_warpage and peak_skewness over those samples only. The struct comment calls these "Peak values across all time". Nothing in the JSON or the report says the values come from a sample. For 992 states the samples are 0,110,220,...,991, so a 40-state window such as 130-170 falls completely between two samples. An inversion that recovers inside that window is never counted. koo_deep_report shows these values as "Peak AR / Min Jac / 음수 Jac" in the quality tab table (html_report.py:1960-1982) and in the console line "음수Jac={n_neg}개" (__main__.py:1403-1410). It also marks cells red only when min_jacobian<0 or max_negative_jacobian_count>0, so a missed inversion shows up as a clean part. The path is used in production but is opt-in: `--element-quality` on koo_deep_report, passed through by scripts/post_analyze.sh:171 or the GUI checkbox (off by default). That fits medium severity.

I could not refute this. It is real. At 36ea5db, processElementQualityJobs gets the full `all_states` vector (UnifiedAnalyzer.cpp:72 reads every state, and :236 passes it in), but it only checks at most 10 evenly spaced states (UnifiedAnalyzer.cpp:1644-1657). ElementQualityStats::computeGlobalStats (AnalysisTypes.hpp:307-359) then works out peak_aspect_ratio, min_jacobian, min/max_volume_change and max_negative_jacobian_count from just those 10 time points. The JSON writer (AnalysisTypes.hpp:731-775) never says the values were sampled: there is no sample count or stride field.

The koo_deep_report HTML table (html_report.py:1958-1982) labels the columns "Peak AR", "Min Jac", "Vol Min/Max" and "음수 Jac", and marks a cell 'crit' only when the value is below 0 or above 0. The console line (__main__.py:1399-1411) prints "음수Jac=N개". Both show these as extremes over the whole run.

For 992 states the checked indices are 0, 110, 220, ... 991. That is about 1% of the states, with gaps of up to 111 states. Any window shorter than about 110 states is never looked at, for example the impact at states 130-170. Short events like this are realistic in drop tests: peak compression at impact, and corner Jacobians that go negative for a while from hourglassing in under-integrated hexes. So the report can show 음수Jac=0 and a mild Min Jac or Peak AR while real inversions happened.

The path is used in production, but only when asked for. It runs when koo_deep_report gets --element-quality, or when a config contains a `type: element_quality` job (__main__.py:364). post_analyze.sh passes the flag through (lines 111 and 171). It is off by default, so medium severity fits.

confirmed.title: Segment-set parent-element lookup sends connectivity values (internal 1-based indices) through the user-node-ID map
confirmed.mechanism: `auto ridx = [&](int32_t nid) { ... nid2idx.find(nid) ... }` where nid2idx maps real_node_ids to index. The map is correct for segment nodes (user IDs), but it is also applied to `for (int32_t nid : mesh.solids[ei].node_ids) { const int32_t ni = ridx(nid); if (ni >= 0) node2elem[ni].push_back(ei); }`. Solid connectivity holds internal 1-based indices; the NodeIndexResolver comment in the same file (l.891-913) says the only correct conversion is nodes[nid-1].
confirmed.scenario: I replicated the logic in Python. Node user IDs are {1..100, 151..250}, i.e. internal 1..200 with a gap. A segment on the bottom face of element 30 (user nodes 175,179,180,176) resolves to parent element 42 instead of 30. Element 3, in the identity range, still resolves correctly. With non-overlapping offsets (e.g. part nodes starting at 100001) the connectivity lookups simply miss: segments are dropped with the misleading note '셸 면이거나 절점 미존재', and set metrics come from a subset or are not computed.
confirmed.consumers: set_reports/<name>/metrics.json and von_mises.csv / eff_plastic_strain.csv for set_type=segment (computeDirectSetMetrics l.1418-1469), plus the parent part candidates used for set views → koo_custom_report html_report.py (peak, peak_element_id).
confirmed.suggested_fix: Build node2elem with `ni = nid - 1` (internal index, range-checked). Keep ridx only for the segment's user node IDs.

verdicts.reason: The defect is real, and I reproduced it on a real d3plot. `GeometryParser` copies the solid connectivity words into `node_ids` without changing them, and in LS-DYNA those words are internal 1-based node numbers. The segment-set branch of `prepareSetReports` builds `node2elem` by passing each connectivity value through `ridx`. `ridx` looks the value up in a map keyed by user node IDs (`real_node_ids`). When `real_node_ids` does not match the internal numbering, the lookup gives the wrong answer. Connectivity values in the renumbered range either miss the map, so the element's nodes never enter `node2elem`, or hit a different node whose user ID happens to equal that internal number. The segment's own node IDs, read from the keyword file, are user IDs and are mapped correctly. So a segment on an element in the renumbered range finds no parent. It is dropped with the misleading note "셸 면이거나 절점 미존재" (shell face or missing node), and the set metrics are either left out or computed from a subset. This branch is reachable in production: koo_custom_report's `runner.py` passes `set_type`/`set_id` from the user's YAML straight to unified_analyzer. Its `metrics.json` is read by koo_custom_report, and by the impact/sphere report code that scans `set_reports/`. The same file's own `NodeIndexResolver` comment (l.891-913) says the correct conversion is `nodes[nid-1]`, and the segment branch was never updated to match. The code around l.1079-1101 is identical in 36ea5db, HEAD and the working tree, so the current binary shows the same behaviour. Severity is medium, not high: a user must configure a segment set, and the deck's node numbering must differ from the internal order.

I could not refute this. The bug is real. The code at 36ea5db runs solid connectivity values through a map built from real_node_ids (user node ID to index). But GeometryParser stores the raw IX8 words without converting them, and those words are LS-DYNA internal 1-based node numbers. The same file already says so in the NodeIndexResolver comment at lines 891-913, which names nodes[nid-1] as the only correct conversion. Segment node IDs from *SET_SEGMENT are user IDs, so ridx is right for them and wrong for the connectivity.

On a deck whose real_node_ids are not identity, the lookup goes wrong in two ways:
1. **Wrong parent:** a connectivity value that happens to match another node's user ID points to the wrong node, so a segment can resolve to the wrong parent element.
2. **Dropped segment:** a connectivity value that matches no user ID is skipped, so the segment is excluded with the misleading note '셸 면이거나 절점 미존재'.

Either way, the per-segment von_mises and eff_plastic_strain series, the peak, the peak_element_id and the parent part candidates can be wrong or computed from only a subset. Nothing downstream checks this. koo_custom_report shows peak_element_id and the values directly (html_report.py:141).

The path is reachable in production: koo_custom_report runner → unified_analyzer set_reports → computeDirectSetMetrics (called at l.205) → metrics.json. Two conditions are needed: set_type=segment, and a deck with non-identity node numbering. Non-identity numbering is realistic; the repo's own comment cites a real deck (NUMNP=29624, non-identity from index 28293). With identity numbering or NARBS=0 both conventions agree, and that limits severity to medium.

- **Averages:** the error equals the eroded fraction, so it is small unless a part erodes heavily.
- **Unaffected here:** strain min, and the report's `min_principal` / `min_principal_strain` (min over time of negative values), do not change. In this deck, eps is already negative in live elements.
- **Global minimum over time:** already 0 at t=0, so it does not change.
- **mean_timemax:** takes the maximum over time, which usually falls before erosion, so it is rarely affected.
- **Element quality:** it does include eroded elements, but I did not quantify it.

The production path is analyze(), called from UnifiedAnalyzer.cpp:312. confirmed.title: All part, motion, surface and quality CSVs are written with std::fixed setprecision(6); fine time steps and small strains/displacements collapse
confirmed.mechanism: writePartCSV: `ofs << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6) << point.time << "," << point.max_value ...` (l.49). writeMotionCSV (l.78), writeSurfaceCSV (l.117) and writeQualityCSV time (l.246) do the same. Only the surface-strain CSV uses scientific.
confirmed.scenario: For time in seconds, 2.5e-6 and 3.5e-6 both print as '0.000003', and 1.0e-7, 1.4e-7, 1.5e-7, 2e-7, 3e-7 and 4e-7 all print as '0.000000' (checked with %.6f). With output intervals of 1e-7..1e-6 s the Time column has duplicate or zero rows. Eff. plastic strain 4.4e-7 → '0.000000'. A principal/vm strain of 3e-9 → '0.000000'. GPa stress 3.2e-5 → '0.000032' (2 significant digits). SI-deck displacement 2e-7 m → '0.000000'.
confirmed.consumers: koo_sphere_report loader reads stress/strain/motion CSVs and computes true_peak/true_peak_time from these strings (loader.py:230-320, 423-452). koo_impact_report builds the impactor trajectory times/velocities from the motion CSV (loader.py:1323-1346) and interpolates matsum KE on those times. koo_deep_report motion CSV parser (d3plot_reader.py:577-615).
confirmed.suggested_fix: Write with std::scientific or std::defaultfloat and setprecision(9) (max_digits10 for float data), as the set-report CSVs already do.

Only writeSurfaceStrainCSV (175) uses scientific. The CSVs from production runs on disk show the loss.

1. **Repeated time values.** In Test_Impact_A (992 states, 1 µs output interval) every CSV has 4 repeated Time values, e.g. rows 151 and 152 are both 0.000153. Test_Postprocess_v14 (about 1.01 µs interval) has 1 per file.

- koo_sphere_report builds TimeSeriesData.true_peak / true_peak_time from the stress, strain and motion CSVs (loader.py:227-320, 423-452). json_report.py:80,88 and html_report.py:174 report time_of_peak from them.

- koo_deep_report parses the motion CSVs and plots them against md.t (html_report.py:232, 1245-1270).
- koo_sphere_report computes true_peak, true_peak_time and true_peak_g_time from the stress, strain and motion CSVs (loader.py:254-265, 294-303).
- koo_impact_report reads the motion CSVs into pm.times (load_per_part_motions). It uses them for the trajectory and for matsum KE interpolation, and np.diff(t) on them sets the FFT and SRS time step (payload/analytics.py:25-29, 181-191).

The FFT time step taken from the mean of the positive diffs then comes out 2x or 10x too large, so the reported dominant frequency is 2x or 10x too low. Medium fits: this is a production path, most numbers are only slightly off at the common 1e-6 s interval, and badly wrong numbers need sub-microsecond output intervals.

confirmed.title: Part-name lookup reads an arbitrary .k file, ignores *INCLUDE and *PART_ variants; a zero-match part_pattern on surface jobs turns into the whole model
confirmed.mechanism: findKeywordFile falls back to the first `fs::directory_iterator(dir)` entry with a .k/.key/.dyn extension. parsePartNamesFromKeyword does not follow *INCLUDE, skips any line containing "*PART_" (l.48: *PART_COMPOSITE, *PART_CONTACT, *PART_INERTIA), and stops after the first PID card. filterPartsByPattern then silently falls back to 'Part_N' names. In processSurfaceStressJobs/processSurfaceStrainJobs, `std::vector<int32_t> target_parts = job.part_ids;` stays empty when the pattern matches nothing, and `extractSolidExteriorSurfaces(target_parts)` with an empty list means all parts.
confirmed.scenario: In /data/battery_study/case_01_phase1_stacked_tier-1 the readdir order returns 07_control_phase1.k first. That file has no *PART; the 34 *PART cards are in 02_mesh_stacked_tier-1.k, pulled in by *INCLUDE from 01_main. Every name pattern matches nothing. A surface_stress job {name: 'PCB bottom', part_pattern: 'PCB*', direction -Z} then reports the -Z surface of the whole model under the name 'PCB bottom'. In koo_custom_report set_reports, a pattern that matches only some parts (others defined via *PART_COMPOSITE or in includes) silently covers a subset; a note is added only when nothing matches.
confirmed.consumers: surface/<job>_stress.csv / _strain.csv and analysis_result.json surface_analysis. koo_custom_report set metrics (resolved_parts, peaks). Render part_pattern selection. part_pattern analysis jobs can be written from the koo_deep_report GUI (gui/app.py:139).
confirmed.suggested_fix: Resolve names from the main deck, following *INCLUDE, and accept *PART_* variants and multi-part *PART blocks. Treat a non-empty pattern that matches 0 parts as an error or a skipped job, never as 'all parts'.

confirmed.defect_class: value computed from truncated series / silent nearest-point substitution
confirmed.title: peak_element_id comes from the 20-point truncated JSON, so it names an element from a different time step
confirmed.mechanism: d3plot_reader._parse_series (line 564) quietly drops the '...(omitted N entries)...' marker: `data = [d for d in raw.get('data', []) if isinstance(d, dict)]`. Only the first 10 and last 10 states are left, and nothing records that the series is incomplete. PartTimeSeries.peak_element_id (models.py:108-117) first looks for an exact time match with time_of_max. If none exists, it silently falls back to `closest = min(self.data, key=lambda d: abs(d['time'] - self.time_of_max)); return closest.get('max_element_id')`. When the peak is in the omitted middle, this returns the max element of state 9 or of state n-10.
confirmed.scenario: Committed sample python/koo_deep_report/single_report/analysis_result.json has 992 states. Part 1 has time_of_max=7.977e-05 and global_max=3748.5 MPa. Running _parse_series plus peak_element_id gives element 4218, which comes from t=9.09e-06, where the max is 0.43 MPa. Parts 2, 3 and 4 also get elements from t=9.09e-06, with maxima of 0.149, 0.234 and 0.034 MPa, against real peaks of 157, 261 and 65.5 MPa. Any run with more than 20 states and a peak outside the first or last 10 states is affected, which covers practically every drop test.
confirmed.consumers: __main__._aggregate line 1332 `peak_element_id=st.peak_element_id` -> PartSummary -> html_report._build_js_data parts[pid].peak_element_id -> Deep Dive KPI card 'peak Element #N / max stress location' (html_report.py:1321-1323). confirmed.suggested_fix: Have unified_analyzer write the element id at the global max (e.g. 'max_element_id_at_peak') next to global_max/time_of_max and read that. At minimum, return None when the exact time_of_max point is missing instead of substituting the nearest surviving point. Also keep a truncation flag on PartTimeSeries so consumers can tell the series is partial.

When the time_of_max point was cut out, PartTimeSeries.peak_element_id finds no exact match and quietly falls back to the nearest surviving point. 2. **`*PART_` variants are skipped.** `*PART_COMPOSITE`, `*PART_CONTACT`, `*PART_INERTIA` and the rest are excluded by `not upper.startswith('*PART_')`.

2. Even when a sample does cross the threshold, `t_engage` snaps to the decimation grid. On real data CID 1 reports 7.97e-5 s when the full-resolution first crossing is 5.99e-5 s.

The splice step adds back just one index, the peak of the summed force over all interfaces. So a short pulse on a secondary interface can fall entirely between kept samples, and its `force_mag_ts` comes out all zeros. confirmed.defect_class: 3 (time quantization in motion CSV consumed without detection)
confirmed.title: Motion CSV Time is written with fixed 6 decimals (1 µs); with output intervals below 1 µs the loader gets duplicate timestamps, and FFT/SRS/t_peak are off by the interval ratio
confirmed.mechanism: Writer examples/unified_analyzer.cpp:78 `ofs << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6) << point.time`. The loader reads it directly with `pm.times.append(fv("Time"))` and never checks for non-increasing time. _fft_dominant_freq (analytics.py:24-31) uses `dts = dts[dts > 0]; dt = mean(dts)`. SRS uses median of positive dts and np.interp over duplicate x. The same Time feeds t_peak_g, TOA and stress-wave velocity. Displacements are also quantized to 1e-6 (1 µm in SI decks).
confirmed.scenario: Output interval 1e-7 s over 2 ms: the 20000 states collapse to 2001 unique times. Reproduced with analytics._fft_dominant_freq: a 20 kHz acceleration signal reports f_dom=20000 Hz with true times and 2000.0 Hz with the CSV-quantized times (fs 1e7 -> 1e6). With the production 1.008e-6 interval, times carry up to 0.5 µs error, e.g. t_first_contact values of exactly 5e-06/1e-05.
confirmed.consumers: deep_analytics.fft (dominant frequency, spectrum), srs, part_motion.t_peak_g, toa dt_ms, stress_wave_velocity, part_motion t_ref charts.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Write Time with std::scientific/setprecision(9), as the surface CSV already does at line 175. In the loader, detect non-strictly-increasing times and flag them rather than feeding FFT/SRS.

No warning is emitted on either path.

MinimumModel_dwit.k sets *DATABASE_BINARY_D3PLOT dt = 1.000e-06 with ENDTIM = 1.000e-03, i.e. the sampling grid coincides with the print grid. Running _fft_dominant_freq on a real CSV (Run_20260603_075506_fe0239/part_9) vs a reconstructed uniform grid gives 991.9 Hz vs 999.0 Hz (0.7 %), below the FFT bin width (1/(N*dt) ~ 1 kHz). So no visibly wrong number reaches a user on the inputs observed today; the defect bites, silently, as soon as a user asks for a finer d3plot interval (<= 5e-7 s in a seconds-unit deck; the audit scope explicitly admits down to 1e-7 s), which is one decade from the current setting. Decks whose time unit is ms are unaffected. Production path, latent, less common input => medium, matching the claim's own severity.

It only matters when the global worst stress is below about 1 in deck units, though. Two cases get there: a GPa deck (kg-mm-ms, a standard LS-DYNA unit system) or a report whose runs are all low-stress. The real production data at /data/koopark/Test_Impact_A is ton-mm-s (MPa), and its payload has worst_s = 2336.5 MPa, where one decimal loses nothing. So typical inputs are unaffected.

The claim's figure of 0.1357 is real, but it is a per-position peak: 16 no-contact positions (F5_DOE_*) each peak at 0.13569176 MPa. It becomes the KPI only if a report is built from those runs alone.

1. **Wrong tile value.** 0.0863 is stored as 0.1, and the s1 tile shows "0.100" (+16%). A value of 0.04 is stored as 0.0 and shows "0.0".
2. **Wrong limit colour, both ways.** The tile compares the rounded value (`k2.worst_s > k2.stress_limit`) against the full-precision limit.
   - False alarm: 0.0863 against a limit of 0.09 turns the tile red.
   - Missed exceedance: 0.1357 against a limit of 0.1 stays uncoloured, because 0.1 is not greater than 0.1. The claim missed this direction, and it is the worse one.
3. **s1 and s9 disagree.** The s9 position table checks each row's full-precision `r.s` against the same limit. In the 0.0863 / 0.09 case the s1 tile is red while no s9 row is red.

The server-rendered value (`:.0f` gives "0") is replaced by JS at boot, so that part is only cosmetic.

- **Aggravating:** the impact report has no kg-mm-ms/GPa unit preset. `_detect_unit_system` puts a kg-mm-ms deck (density 7.85e-6, lengths in mm) under ton-mm-s and labels its stress "MPa", so a GPa deck's KPI is already mislabelled before this rounding.
- **Another consumer:** koo_federate_report copies the impact `kpi` into `sidecar_kpi` and shows worst_s with 0 decimals.

Medium severity fits: production path, but it needs uncommon input.

The claim holds. At 36ea5db, `ImpactReport.sim_params` is a plain `dict` (models.py:390). `getattr(dict, "yield_stress_by_part", None)` always returns the default, so `yield_map` is always `{}` and `has_yield` is always False. Every part therefore takes the composite branch.

confirmed.defect_class: 6 (silently dropping entries so the DOE looks complete)
confirmed.title: DOE discovery silently skips runs without step_config.txt or without d3plot/deep output, and the report never knows they existed
confirmed.mechanism: `if not cfg_path.exists(): continue` (1987) and `if not d3plot.exists() and deep_dir is None: continue` (1990, same at 2065/2098). No warning and no load_issue. load_partial_impact_doe_report sets `n_runs=len(runs)` and `n_failed` only from discovered runs, and does not compare against scenario grid nx*ny (read only as a hint at 2596-2604) or jobs.json.
confirmed.scenario: A 5x5 DOE where 2 jobs are still pending/cancelled (Run dir with step_config but no Output/d3plot yet) or whose Output was cleaned: the report shows n_positions=23 and 'Runs failed to load' is absent. KPIs, safe-zone counts and the 'n_valid_runs 9/23' badge describe 23 runs as the whole DOE, and grid cells for the missing positions are just empty.
confirmed.consumers: kpi.n_positions/n_safe, analyzer findings (n_runs denominators), DOE grid/heatmaps, impact_report.json doe_config.n_runs.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Record skipped Run_* dirs as load_issues (kind 'run-skipped' with reason) and count them in n_runs/n_failed. Warn when discovered positions != grid nx*ny.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this claim. The mechanism is real and runs in production. `_discover_test_impact_runs` silently skips any Run_* dir that has no step_config.txt, and any run that has neither a d3plot nor a reusable deep_report output (loader.py:1987-1988, 1990-1991, 2065-2066, 2097-2099). None of these skips prints a warning or records a load_issue.

`load_partial_impact_doe_report` then treats only the runs it found as the whole DOE. It computes `n_failed` from those runs only (2512) and sets `doe_config.n_runs = len(runs)` (2621). The analyzer uses that count as the denominator in its findings and raises "Runs failed to load" only from `run-load-failed` issues.

The scenario grid (nx, ny) is copied into `sim_params["grid"]` (2596-2604) but is only used to place cells. I found no check anywhere in koo_impact_report or scripts/ that compares the expected nx*ny, or jobs.json, against the positions actually loaded. post_analyze.sh (`run_step_impact` / `should_skip_unified_for_impact`) calls `koo_impact_report --test-dir`, which sends flat layouts to this loader, so the path is live.

A stubbed test reproduced it. Real data has the trigger too: /data/koopark/Test_impback_job/output has 3 Run_* dirs, each with step_config.txt and an Output/ dir that holds only lsdyna_stdout.log, fort.* and the deck, with no d3plot. So runs that die before writing a d3plot, or are still pending, really occur.

Limits on the claim: a run that crashes after writing any d3plot is still included. If every run lacks a d3plot, the loader raises "No usable runs found" instead of loading silently. The silent under-count needs a mix of complete and missing runs. I did not verify the "n_valid_runs 9/23" badge wording from the claim. Medium severity fits.

The claim holds. I read loader.py at 36ea5db and ran the real loader against a fake 5-position DOE, replacing only the per-run worker with a stub. Two ways a run gets dropped without any trace: its Run_* dir has no step_config.txt, or it has neither Output/d3plot nor reusable deep_report output. Nothing is printed, no load_issue is recorded, and nothing counts it. This happens in _discover_test_impact_runs, before the report knows the run exists. So n_runs, n_failed and n_positions all come from the runs that were found. The analyzer's "Runs failed to load" finding reads only 'run-load-failed' load_issues, so it never fires. The scenario grid nx/ny is used only to lay out the heatmap and interpolation grid. It is never compared with the number of positions found. The report does not read jobs.json at all; the docstring only lists it as optional. Nothing else in the code protects the user either. __main__ calls the same discovery. post_analyze.sh only checks that at least one d3plot exists (find ... | head -1) before running koo_impact_report. In the DOE grid, a missing cell looks like an empty '·' cell and is not marked as a missing run. Realistic ways to hit this: a DOE job that died before its first d3plot was written (deck/input error, license failure, Slurm cancel or timeout, node failure), or a report run while some jobs are still pending. This contradicts the module's own P1b rule that load problems must reach load_issues instead of disappearing. The docstring describes the filtering on purpose, but not surfacing the skipped runs is the defect. Medium severity: it is on the production path, but it needs failed or pending runs. Minor correction: the lines are 1987-1988 and 1990-1991 (flat layout) and 2065-2066 and 2098-2099 (KooChainRun DWI layout), off by one from the claim.

confirmed.title: Tier C (101-300 positions) keeps energy flows and acceleration curves for only the top 40 positions with no chunks and no notice; the energy panel silently keeps the previous position
confirmed.mechanism: `if _topk > 0 and len(_ef_items) > _topk: ... _ef_items = _ef_items[:_topk]` and `_topk_pos = ...[:_tier.part_motion_topk]` (lines 488-495), with tier C emit_mode 'deferred', so emit.py writes no chunk files. s3_verdict.py:830 `if (!flows[posId]) return;   // 흐름 없는 위치면 현 상태 유지`. s9 shows 'no acc time series' for positions outside the top 40. No JS text mentions the cap.
confirmed.scenario: A 150-position DOE: selecting the 41st-ranked position in s9 leaves the energy graph/Sankey/conservation panels showing the previously selected position's flow, and the acceleration chart says the series does not exist although it was computed and dropped.
confirmed.consumers: s3 energy-flow panels, s9 per-position charts, s4 per-part G chart.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Write chunks for tier C too, or clear the panel with an explicit 'dropped by tier cap (top-40)' message. Add the cap to the payload meta and show it.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute the claim. At 36ea5db the code works as described. With 101 to 300 positions, tier_for returns tier C: emit_mode "deferred", energy_flow_topk=40, part_motion_topk=40. In emit_report, chunk files are only written when mode == "chunked", so a tier C report has no DATA.chunks. The payload keeps energy flows only for the 40 positions with the largest energy_dissipated, and inline acceleration series only for the 40 worst-peak_g positions. Nothing is written to the payload meta to record the cap.

On the energy page, refreshEnergyFlowForPos returns early for a dropped position. All 7 panels keep showing the previous position's flow and no explanation appears. One detail softens the claim: the efd-pos-label header also keeps the old position id, so the panel is still labelled correctly. The energy panel therefore shows no wrong numbers. The problem is that it silently stops following the selection.

The acceleration chart in s9 is a real misstatement. With no chunks, renderS9 calls renderS9Charts(posId, null). That filters the inline series, finds none and prints "가속도 시계열 없음" / "no acc time series". Those series were loaded and computed, then dropped by the cap. I grepped sections/ and assets/ and found no text that mentions the 40-position cap or the tier.

This is reachable in production. The CLI picks the tier automatically, and a DOE with 101 to 300 positions is realistic: the code comments refer to 338-position runs. Passing --single-file with more than 100 positions gives the same caps with no chunks. Tier D (more than 300 positions) has the same energy-flow cap, because build_position_bundle chunks hold only motion and trajectory data, not energy flows. Nothing wrong reaches a KPI value. The damage is missing data presented as "does not exist" or as a panel that silently stops updating, and it needs a larger DOE. Medium severity is appropriate.

The claim holds at 36ea5db. I built a synthetic report with 150 positions and ran the commit's own `_build_payload` on it. The mode resolved to 'deferred' (tier C) with no `chunks` key. Only 40 of 150 energy_flows were kept, and part_motion series covered only 40 of 150 positions. Nothing in the payload mentions the cap. The JS never mentions it either (checked s3, s4, s9 and the js_core badges).

s9 path: `renderS9` finds no inline series and no `DATA.chunks`, so it calls `renderS9Charts(posId, null)`. That prints '가속도 시계열 없음' ('no acc time series') for any position outside the worst 40 by peak_g. The series was computed and then dropped, so the chart wrongly says it does not exist.

s3 path: `selectPosition` calls `refreshEnergyFlowForPos(posId)`, which returns at `if (!flows[posId]) return;`. The energy graph, Sankey, conservation and contact-trust panels keep showing the previous position, with no message.

One limit on the claim: the `efd-pos-label` header is not updated either, so it still names the old position. The panels are therefore never labelled with the wrong position ID. The data just silently fails to follow the selection. The code comment admits this ('나머지 위치를 s9 에서 고르면 refreshEnergyFlowForPos 가 조용히 현 상태를 유지한다'), but users are never told.

The energy-flow cap reaches further than the claim says. Tier D (>300 positions) and `--chunked` also set `energy_flow_topk=40`, and `build_position_bundle` never writes energy flows into chunk files. So in every tier C/D report, flows for all but 40 positions are unrecoverable.

This is production-reachable: `loader.py` DOE mode fills `energy_flows[pos_id]` and `part_motions` for every run, and `__main__` picks the tier automatically. Severity is medium. No wrong number is attributed to a position, but for realistic 101-300 position DOEs, computed data is dropped and shown as nonexistent or silently stale, with no notice.

confirmed.title: Contact-sequence timeline hard-codes a 0-1 ms time axis and samples only 21 indices of the contact mask
confirmed.mechanism: Header `(i % 5 === 0) ? (i / 20).toFixed(1) : ''` and cell title `'t=' + (i / 20).toFixed(2) + ' ms'` (line 747) regardless of the trajectory's actual t, while cells take `idx = Math.floor(i * (T - 1) / 20)` from the downsampled contact array.
confirmed.scenario: Test_DropWeight_Validation (tFinal=0.002 s) and fullangle decks (0.005 s): a contact at 1.5 ms is shown under the '0.8 ms' label, and Test_DWI (tFinal 0.5 ms) is stretched to '1.0 ms'. A contact shorter than record/20 (e.g. 40 µs in a 1 ms record) can fall between sampled indices and show 'free flight'.
confirmed.consumers: s5 Contact Sequence Timeline (top-8 positions).
confirmed.suggested_fix: Derive labels and cell times from tr.t (t0..t_end in the declared unit). Mark a cell engaged if any sample in its time bin is engaged (OR over the bin) instead of point-sampling.

verdicts.reason: Mechanism verified at 36ea5db and reachable in the shipped report. initContactTimeline (s5_doe.py:686-748) is called from the s3 lazy init (report/assets/js_core.py:652) and its panel markup is s3_verdict.py:203; the generated production report /data/koopark/Test_Impact_A/impact_report.html contains 'cseq-grid', 'CONTACT ENGAGEMENT SEQUENCE' and the literal source "t=' + (i / 20).toFixed(2) + ' ms". (1) Point sampling loses real contact: replaying line 721/722 against the real payload, position F5_DOE_015 - which ranks 6th under the same FACE_POS_MAX-by-g top-8 selection at s5_doe.py:694-701, i.e. it IS displayed - has two contact intervals (0.006-0.067 ms and 0.151-0.164 ms) that fall entirely between sampled indices and render as 'free flight'; a bin-OR would mark those cells CONTACT. Other runs lose up to 6 intervals (F5_DOE_022). So a wrong cell already reaches a user today. (2) The time label derives solely from the cell index and never from tr.t, which IS present in the payload (report/payload/__init__.py:402). In Test_Impact_A records end at exactly 1.0 ms so labels coincidentally match; for other record lengths the label is wrong, and such decks exist in the same discovery layout (ENDTIM 5.000e-04 in Test_DWI, 2.000e-03 in Test_DropWeight_Validation, 0.005 in Test_Impact_A's other deck), all picked up by loader._discover_test_impact_runs' flat-DOE output/Run_* scan. Minor correction to the claim: the header cells at line 708 print unit-less fractions 0.0..1.0 (no 'ms'), so the explicit unit assertion is only the tooltip at line 747; both still ignore tr.t. Payload unit_labels.time is 's'. Nothing elsewhere clamps or rescales the trajectory time base, and the panel caption only says '21 timesteps'.

Both halves of the claim reproduce.

(1) Hard-coded 0–1 ms axis. `initContactTimeline()` builds the header and every cell tooltip from the loop counter alone — `(i/20).toFixed(1)` for the header and `'t=' + (i/20).toFixed(2) + ' ms'` for the tooltip — while the cell itself is taken from `idx = Math.floor(i*(T-1)/20)`, i.e. a fraction of the trajectory array, not of a 1 ms window. `tr.t` (the real time vector, seconds, present in the same TRAJ object) is never consulted, and no other code rewrites those labels (`cseq-grid` is only touched here; confirmed by grep over the whole package and over a shipped report). So the label is correct only when the record happens to be exactly 1 ms. That is the pyKooCAE default (`impact_params.get('tFinal', 0.001)`), and Test_Impact_A decks indeed have `ENDTIM 1.000e-03` — but tFinal is a scenario parameter and real test sets on this machine use other values: /data/koopark/Test_DWI/.../DropWeightImpactTestSet.k has `ENDTIM 5.000e-04` and /data/koopark/Test_DropWeight_Validation/.../DropWeightImpactTestSet.k has `ENDTIM 2.000e-03`. Both layouts (`output/Run_*` and KooChainRun `output/results/dwi_*/Run_*`) are handled by `_discover_test_impact_runs`, so both are production inputs for koo_impact_report. On the 2 ms deck a contact at t=1.5 ms lands in cell 15 and hovers as "t=0.75 ms" (verified formatting in node: header ticks render 0.0/0.3/0.5/0.8/1.0, tooltip for i=15 is "t=0.75 ms"); on the 0.5 ms DWI deck the record is stretched to a "1.0 ms" end label. The unit suffix is also hard-coded ' ms' while `DATA.unit_labels.time` is "s" in the real payload, so it is not even routed through `_u('time')` the way the rest of the file is.

(2) 21-point sampling of the contact mask. The cell is point-sampled (`tr.contact[idx]`), not OR-ed over the bin, so any contact bout shorter than the bin (≈ T/20 samples) can vanish. Reproduced on real production data — the 25-position trajectories parsed out of /data/koopark/Test_Impact_A/impact_report.html (T≈332 samples over 1 ms, bin ≈ 0.05 ms): position F5_DOE_022 is engaged in 70/332 samples yet only 2 of 21 cells light up; bin-OR gives 6. Cells 3,4,5 (real t = 0.148/0.200/0.248 ms) are painted "free flight" although contact exists inside each of those bins. Even near-continuous contacts lose cells: F5_DOE_013 (314/332 engaged, a genuine top-8 "bounce" row) shows "free flight" at cell 2 (t≈0.097 ms), F5_DOE_015 at cell 3 (t≈0.145 ms). Contact runs as short as 0.003–0.03 ms in these files are invisible entirely.

The panel is reachable: `initContactTimeline()` is called from the s3 lazy init block (js_core.py:652), the markup `<div class="cseq-grid" id="cseq-grid">` is in s3_verdict.py:203, and both the header expression and the tooltip expression are present verbatim in the already-generated production report /data/koopark/Test_Impact_A/impact_report.html.

I keep the claimed severity at medium rather than high: on the default 1 ms decks — which is what the flagship Test_Impact_A set uses — the time labels coincide with reality, so the wrong-time reading needs a non-default tFinal (real but less common), and the false "free-flight" cells are a qualitative map whose quantitative counterpart (t_first_contact, the contact-band shading in the per-position detail) is shown elsewhere. Adjacent instances of the same hard-coded-time class in the same file, not part of this claim: s5_doe.py:660-662 annotates the phase diagram at literal 0.1e-3/0.3e-3/0.5e-3/1.0e-3 s by nearest sample, so on a 0.5 ms record the "1.0 ms" dot is drawn on the last sample at 0.5 ms; and s5_doe.py:943 prints `(tr.t_first_contact*1000).toFixed(2)` with the unit label `_u('time')` = "s", rendering 1e-5 s as "0.01 s" instead of 0.01 ms.

Worst case: Run_20260207_225111_ac4ff7 part 10, true 139,029 G vs 16,928 G in g_ts (12%). For stress, median is 85% of true and worst is Run_20260207_215839_edb467 part 14, 227.6 MPa true vs 61.5 MPa (27%). confirmed.consumers: koo_sphere_report report.html: Impact Analysis tab (phase timing table and scatter, hot-spot element table), Advanced tab (Impact Pulse KPIs/table, Critical Element, Rebound, Crack Arrest CAI), Part Deep Dive time-domain section, Time History charts.
